docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil, final judgment)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil, final judgment): 30 days from entry of the judgment on the docket (Supr. Ct. R. 6(a)(i); 10 Del. C. §§ 145, 148). Cannot be enlarged (Supr. Ct. R. 11(b)).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Cross-appeal
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Cross-appeal: 15 days from filing of the first notice of appeal (or 30 days from judgment, whichever is later) (Supr. Ct. R. 6(b)(i); 10 Del. C. § 149).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Challenge to a Delaware Rapid Arbitration Act final award
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Challenge to a Delaware Rapid Arbitration Act final award: 15 days from issuance of the final award (Supr. Ct. R. 6(a)(ii)). Cross-challenge: 7 days after the first notice is served, or 15 days after the award, whichever is later.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Application to certify an interlocutory appeal (trial court)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Application to certify an interlocutory appeal (trial court): 10 days from entry of the interlocutory order (Supr. Ct. R. 42(c)(i)). The trial court may allow longer for good cause.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Notice of interlocutory appeal (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Notice of interlocutory appeal (Supreme Court): 30 days from entry of the interlocutory order (Supr. Ct. R. 42(d)(i); 10 Del. C. § 143). File even if the trial court has not ruled on certification.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP (UPEPA) motion
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP (UPEPA) motion: 10 days from entry of the order (10 Del. C. § 6009). Applies to actions filed or claims asserted on or after Sept. 15, 2025.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Disclosure of corporate affiliations (Form P)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Disclosure of corporate affiliations (Form P): 15 days from notice of docketing of the appeal (Supr. Ct. R. 7(g)).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Opening brief and appendix
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Opening brief and appendix: 30 days from filing of the record (or 45 days after the notice of appeal if no transcript is designated) (Supr. Ct. R. 15(a)(i)).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Answering brief
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Answering brief: 30 days from service of the opening brief (Supr. Ct. R. 15(a)(ii)).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Reply brief: 15 days from service of the answering brief (Supr. Ct. R. 15(a)(iii)). 30 days if the reply also answers a cross-appeal; cross-appellee’s reply 10 days after that.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Motion to extend a briefing deadline
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Motion to extend a briefing deadline: 5 days from before the due date (must be docketed at least 5 days in advance) (Supr. Ct. R. 15(b)(i)). Counted backward from the due date.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Motion for reargument (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Motion for reargument (Supreme Court): 15 days from filing of the opinion or order (Supr. Ct. R. 18).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Motion for rehearing en banc
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Motion for rehearing en banc: 15 days from filing of the panel’s opinion or order (Supr. Ct. R. 4(f)). Not available if the panel ordered the mandate to issue forthwith.

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — Reargument in the trial court (Superior Court or Chancery)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. Reargument in the trial court (Superior Court or Chancery): 5 days from filing of the decision (Super. Ct. Civ. R. 59(e); Ct. Ch. R. 59(c)).

docs.t: Delaware appeal deadline — New trial or motion to alter or amend (trial court)
docs.x: Delaware appellate deadline. New trial or motion to alter or amend (trial court): 10 days from entry of judgment (Super. Ct. Civ. R. 59(b), (d); Ct. Ch. R. 59(a)–(b)). Not the federal 28 days.

docs.t: Georgia — Discovery must be finished within 6 months of the answer to use the court’s compulsory process
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Discovery must be finished within 6 months of the answer to use the court’s compulsory process: Under USCR 5.1, discovery must be started promptly and completed within 6 months after the answer is filed (or 6 months starting 30 days after service if no timely answer) for a party to use the court’s compulsory process to compel it. The court may open, extend, reopen, or shorten the period, but ask before it closes. Motions to compel must quote or attach each request and response and certify a good-faith conference. (USCR 5.1, 6.4)

docs.t: Georgia — Responses to motions are due in 30 days, and there is no hearing unless you ask
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Responses to motions are due in 30 days, and there is no hearing unless you ask: Responses are due 30 days after service of a motion (not 14). Civil motions, including summary judgment, are decided without oral hearing unless the court orders otherwise; for summary judgment, a separate “Request for Oral Hearing” must be filed with the motion or within 5 days after the response time. Summary-judgment motions need a separate statement of material facts, and the response needs its own statement of disputed facts. (USCR 6.2, 6.3, 6.5)

docs.t: Georgia — Email the judge when you e-file a motion
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Email the judge when you e-file a motion: When a motion or response is e-filed, the filer must notify the opposing parties and the assigned judge (or the judge’s designee) by email contemporaneously and no later than 24 hours after e-filing. Every pre-trial motion must also include citations of authority and, for unstipulated facts, affidavits or record citations. (USCR 6.1)

docs.t: Georgia — Recusal motions: 5 days from learning, 10 days before the hearing
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Recusal motions: 5 days from learning, 10 days before the hearing: A superior court recusal motion must be filed and presented within 5 days after learning the grounds and at least 10 days before the hearing or trial, with a specific affidavit. Conclusory affidavits fail, and the motion cannot delay the proceeding. (USCR 25.1–25.2)

docs.t: Georgia — Interlocutory appeal needs a trial-court certificate and a 10-day application, with no extensions
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Interlocutory appeal needs a trial-court certificate and a 10-day application, with no extensions: Most non-final orders reach the appellate courts only by application after the trial court signs a certificate of immediate review. The application is due within 10 days after the certificate is entered (filed with the clerk). Neither appellate court grants extensions for interlocutory applications or responses, and if granted, a notice of appeal must be filed in the trial court within 10 days of the grant order. The statutory time to obtain the certificate is in O.C.G.A. § 5-6-34(b) (not collected). (Ga. Ct. App. R. 16(d), 30(a), (h), (j); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 30)

docs.t: Georgia — Some final judgments are appealable only by discretionary application
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Some final judgments are appealable only by discretionary application: For case types listed in O.C.G.A. § 5-6-35 (statute not collected; divorce decrees are one example the rules mention), the appeal is by application filed in the appellate court within 30 days after the order is entered (7 days for dispossessory orders under O.C.G.A. § 44-7-56). An extension is possible only by motion filed on or before the due date. If granted, file the notice of appeal within 10 days. (Ga. Ct. App. R. 31(a), (b), (h), (j); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 33–34)

docs.t: Georgia — Court of Appeals reconsideration motions are due by 4:30 p.m., not midnight
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Court of Appeals reconsideration motions are due by 4:30 p.m., not midnight: Most e-filings in the Court of Appeals count as filed through 11:59 p.m., but a motion for reconsideration must be received by 4:30 p.m. within 10 days after the judgment; later filings count as received the next business day. Extensions only for providential cause by motion before the 10 days run. Mail-box and prison-mailbox rules do not apply. (Ga. Ct. App. R. 4(b)–(d), 37(b), 46(a))

docs.t: Georgia — Certiorari takes two filings in two courts
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Certiorari takes two filings in two courts: To seek Supreme Court review of a Court of Appeals decision, first file a notice of intent to apply for certiorari in the Court of Appeals within 10 days after judgment (or after the ruling on reconsideration), then file the petition in the Supreme Court within 20 days after judgment or the reconsideration ruling, and file notice of the petition in the Court of Appeals the same day. A motion for permission to file a second reconsideration motion does not toll the 10 days. (Ga. Ct. App. R. 37(d), 38(a); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 38)

docs.t: Georgia — Leaves of absence work in trial courts but not in the appellate courts
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Leaves of absence work in trial courts but not in the appellate courts: In superior court, a lawyer can protect cases with a USCR 16.1 notice filed at least 30 days before a leave of 30 cumulative days or less; it stands granted unless opposing counsel objects or the court denies it within ten days. Longer leaves need a USCR 16.2 application. A leave never extends a deadline set by law or the court. The Court of Appeals and the Supreme Court do not recognize leaves of absence at all. (USCR 16.1–16.3; Ga. Ct. App. R. 9(f); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 4(10))

docs.t: Georgia — Withdrawal requires a 20-day client notice with prescribed contents
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Withdrawal requires a 20-day client notice with prescribed contents: To withdraw in superior court, give the client written notice with the items listed in USCR 4.3(2) (including the client’s right to object within 20 days and the exact 20th day), file a notification certificate, and then request an order. The request is granted as of course only if made before a pretrial order is entered; the judge may refuse it if it would delay a trial on a published calendar, disrupt the court, or be manifestly unfair to the client. Substitution of counsel can instead be done by a notice signed by the party and the new lawyer. (USCR 4.3(1)–(3))

docs.t: Georgia — Pro hac vice: appearing before approval can sink later applications
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Pro hac vice: appearing before approval can sink later applications: A court should deny pro hac vice if the applicant previously filed or appeared in a Georgia court without approval under the USCR, and frequent appearances can be treated as regular practice. The annual $200 fee is due January 15 for every year you remain admitted in any Georgia case. (USCR 4.4 D.3(d)–(e), E.3; Ga. R. Prof. Conduct 5.5 (pro hac vice fee paragraph))

docs.t: Georgia — Default judgments need a written service certificate
docs.x: Georgia land mine. Default judgments need a written service certificate: A party seeking default judgment must attach to the proposed judgment a written certificate stating the date and type of service, whether proof of service was filed within 5 business days of service (or when it was filed), that no defensive pleading appears of record, and the defendant’s military status if required. (USCR 15)

docs.t: Georgia anti-SLAPP — Procedure, deadlines, discovery stay, and fees: confirm in the code
docs.x: Georgia anti-SLAPP. Procedure, deadlines, discovery stay, and fees: confirm in the code: Not verified from collected text. Practitioners commonly describe § 9-11-11.1 as requiring the special motion to strike to be filed within a short period after service of the complaint, staying discovery while the motion is pending, requiring a prompt hearing, and awarding attorney’s fees to a prevailing moving defendant. Treat every one of those points (and any day count) as unconfirmed until checked against the current code text; later sessions (2017–2024) were not checked for amendments. (O.C.G.A. § 9-11-11.1 (text not collected))

docs.t: Georgia anti-SLAPP — Appeal: direct appeal of anti-SLAPP rulings
docs.x: Georgia anti-SLAPP. Appeal: direct appeal of anti-SLAPP rulings: Per the 2016 summary, the Act amended O.C.G.A. § 5-6-34 to allow a direct appeal of an order or judgment on an anti-SLAPP claim or motion, so no certificate of immediate review or interlocutory application should be needed. Confirm the current wording of § 5-6-34, which was amended again in 2025 (HB 176, SB 298, HB 155). (O.C.G.A. § 5-6-34 (as amended by 2016 Act 420); 2025 Legislative Counsel summary)

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (direct appeal)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (direct appeal): 30 days from Entry of the appealable judgment or order (O.C.G.A. § 5-6-38 (statute not collected)). Not verified from collected text; confirm in the code, including tolling by motion for new trial, motion in arrest of judgment, or motion for judgment notwithstanding the verdict.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Extension of notice-of-appeal deadline
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Extension of notice-of-appeal deadline: None days from Must be requested before the original period expires (Ga. Ct. App. R. 16(a); O.C.G.A. § 5-6-39). Only one extension, not longer than the original period; try the trial court first.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Interlocutory application
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Interlocutory application: 10 days from Entry of the order granting the certificate of immediate review (Ga. Ct. App. R. 30(a); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 30). No extensions. The time for the trial court to sign the certificate is in O.C.G.A. § 5-6-34(b) (not collected).

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Response to interlocutory or discretionary application
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Response to interlocutory or discretionary application: 10 days from Docketing of the application (Ga. Ct. App. R. 30(i), 31(i); Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 30, 33). Optional unless ordered; no extensions in the Court of Appeals.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Discretionary application
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Discretionary application: 30 days from Entry (filing) of the trial court order (Ga. Ct. App. R. 31(a)). 7 days for dispossessory orders (O.C.G.A. § 44-7-56). Extension only by motion filed on or before the due date.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Notice of appeal after an application is granted
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Notice of appeal after an application is granted: 10 days from Order granting the application (Ga. Ct. App. R. 30(j), 31(j)). File in the trial court.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief (Court of Appeals): 20 days from Docketing (Ga. Ct. App. R. 23(a)). Extension motion must be filed before the due date.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief (Court of Appeals): 40 days from Docketing, or 20 days after appellant’s brief if later (Ga. Ct. App. R. 23(b)). Required of the State in criminal appeals.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Reply brief (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Reply brief (Court of Appeals): 20 days from Filing of appellee’s brief (Ga. Ct. App. R. 23(c)). One reply only; 4,200 words.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief (Supreme Court): 20 days from Docketing (or order granting certiorari) (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 10(1)(a), 45). Same for cross-appellant from cross-appeal docketing.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief (Supreme Court): 40 days from Docketing, or 20 days after appellant’s brief if later (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 10(1)(b)).

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Reply brief (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Reply brief (Supreme Court): 50 days from Docketing, or 10 days after the response brief if later (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 10(2)). 7,000 words.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Oral argument request (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Oral argument request (Court of Appeals): 20 days from Docketing (Ga. Ct. App. R. 28(a)(2)). Not extended by a brief extension.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Oral argument request (Supreme Court, appellant)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Oral argument request (Supreme Court, appellant): 20 days from Docketing (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 51(1)). Appellee: within 10 days after appellant’s brief is filed. Renew within 5 days after a transfer.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Motion for reconsideration (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Motion for reconsideration (Court of Appeals): 10 days from Judgment or dismissal (Ga. Ct. App. R. 37(b)). Must be received by 4:30 p.m.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Motion for reconsideration (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Motion for reconsideration (Supreme Court): 10 days from The ruling (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 13(3), 27(2)). Must be received or e-filed within the 10 days; no mailbox rule.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Notice of intent to apply for certiorari (filed in Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Notice of intent to apply for certiorari (filed in Court of Appeals): 10 days from Judgment, or order ruling on reconsideration (Ga. Ct. App. R. 38(a)(1)).

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Petition for certiorari (filed in Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Petition for certiorari (filed in Supreme Court): 20 days from Judgment, or disposition of reconsideration motion (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 38(2)). File notice of the petition in the Court of Appeals the same day.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Response to certiorari petition
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Response to certiorari petition: 20 days from Filing of the petition (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 42). Reply within 10 days after the response (Rule 42.1).

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Notice of intent to seek U.S. Supreme Court certiorari (filed in Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Notice of intent to seek U.S. Supreme Court certiorari (filed in Court of Appeals): 20 days from Supreme Court of Georgia’s denial of certiorari (Ga. Ct. App. R. 38(b)(1)). Generally does not stay the remittitur.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Recusal motion (Court of Appeals)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Recusal motion (Court of Appeals): 20 days from Docketing (Ga. Ct. App. R. 44(a)). Unless good cause shown.

docs.t: Georgia appeal deadline — Recusal motion (Supreme Court)
docs.x: Georgia appellate deadline. Recusal motion (Supreme Court): 5 days from Learning of the grounds (Ga. Sup. Ct. R. 26(2)). And no later than 10 days before oral argument.

docs.t: Guam — Post-judgment motions: 10 days, counted on the calendar since October 2023
docs.x: Guam land mine. Post-judgment motions: 10 days, counted on the calendar since October 2023: Renewed judgment as a matter of law, amended findings, new trial, and motions to alter or amend the judgment are all due no later than 10 days after entry of judgment. Federal practice allows 28 days. The court cannot extend these deadlines. Since PRM 06-006-24 (Oct. 19, 2023), GRCP 6(a) counts every day, including weekends and holidays, so the 10 days are calendar days. A Rule 60 motion tolls the appeal time only if filed within 10 days after judgment. (GRCP 6(a)(1), 6(b)(2), 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e); GRAP 4(a)(4)(A)(vi))

docs.t: Guam — Statement of jurisdiction within 10 days of the notice of appeal, or the appeal is dismissed
docs.x: Guam land mine. Statement of jurisdiction within 10 days of the notice of appeal, or the appeal is dismissed: Within 10 days after filing the notice of appeal, the appellant must submit a statement of jurisdiction to the Supreme Court. It must give the basis for finality or appealability, the statutory basis for jurisdiction, and the docket-entry date, with a legible copy of the judgment showing its entry date. If it is not filed, or if it shows no final appealable judgment has been entered, the appeal is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction. Within the same 10 days, order the transcript (or certify none) and file the representation statement. (GRAP 4.1(a)–(b), 7(b)(1), 8(b))

docs.t: Guam — Two clocks: the Supreme Court skips weekends for short periods, the Superior Court does not
docs.x: Guam land mine. Two clocks: the Supreme Court skips weekends for short periods, the Superior Court does not: GRAP 11(a)(1)(B) still excludes Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays from periods shorter than 11 days, unless stated as calendar days. GRCP 6(a), as amended in 2023, counts every day. A 10-day deadline in the Supreme Court can therefore end days later than a 10-day deadline in the Superior Court. GRAP adds 3 calendar days after service, including electronic service. GRCP adds 3 days after service by mail, clerk-leaving or consented means, including e-service. (GRAP 11(a)(1), 11(c); GRCP 6(a), 6(d))

docs.t: Guam — Answer in 20 days; Government of Guam gets 60; serve within 90
docs.x: Guam land mine. Answer in 20 days; Government of Guam gets 60; serve within 90: A defendant must answer within 20 days after service of the summons and complaint. The Government of Guam and its officers or agencies get 60 days after service on the Attorney General or agency counsel. After a ruling on a Rule 12 motion, the responsive pleading is due within 10 days. A plaintiff must serve within 90 days after filing; this was 180 days before October 19, 2023. A waiver request must allow 30 days (60 if the defendant is outside Guam). (GRCP 12(a), 4(d)(1)(F), 4(m))

docs.t: Guam — Motion briefing runs from the motion’s filing date, and oral argument must be requested
docs.x: Guam land mine. Motion briefing runs from the motion’s filing date, and oral argument must be requested: In Superior Court civil cases, an opposition is due 28 days after the motion is filed, not after service. The reply is due 42 days after the motion is filed. Parties may extend each by stipulation by no more than 7 days, and late papers are not considered without leave. Memoranda are limited to 20 pages and replies to 10. Request oral argument on the notice of motion or Form 2 within 7 days after the last paper is due. If you do not, the request is waived and the court may rule on the papers. (CVR 7.1(d), (e)(2)–(3), (f), (g))

docs.t: Guam — One set of interrogatories, 50 questions; discovery motions need a joint stipulation
docs.x: Guam land mine. One set of interrogatories, 50 questions; discovery motions need a joint stipulation: Without leave, each party may serve only one set of interrogatories and one set of requests for admission on any other party. Each set is capped at 50 including every subpart. Answers must quote each question in full. Before any discovery motion, counsel must meet and confer. If disputes remain, they must file with the motion a written stipulation setting out each issue verbatim with each side’s contentions; otherwise the court will not hear the motion. GRCP 26(b)(1) still uses the pre-2015 scope (“reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence”), with no proportionality language. (CVR 33.1(a)–(b), 37.1(a)–(b); GRCP 26(b)(1), 33(a))

docs.t: Guam — Jury demand within 10 days after the last pleading
docs.x: Guam land mine. Jury demand within 10 days after the last pleading: A jury must be demanded in writing and served no later than 10 days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue. Failure to serve and file the demand waives a jury. GRCP 6(a) now counts those 10 days on the calendar. (GRCP 38(b), (d); GRCP 6(a))

docs.t: Guam — Appeal mechanics: file in the Superior Court and pay the Supreme Court’s fee at the same time
docs.x: Guam land mine. Appeal mechanics: file in the Superior Court and pay the Supreme Court’s fee at the same time: The notice of appeal is filed with the Clerk of the Superior Court within 30 days after entry of the judgment or order. The appellant must also send the Supreme Court a file-stamped copy. The non-refundable Supreme Court docket fee ($375 on the posted schedule) is paid to the Clerk of the Supreme Court when the notice is filed below, and a cross-appellant pays its own fee. A second party may appeal within 14 days after the first notice. (GRAP 3(a), 4(a)(1), (3), 8(a); Supreme Court of Guam Filing Fee Schedule)

docs.t: Guam — Pro hac vice does not follow the case up on appeal
docs.x: Guam land mine. Pro hac vice does not follow the case up on appeal: Admission in the Superior Court does not carry over to the Supreme Court. File a new verified application there; no second fee is charged for the same lawyer in the same case. Your Guam sponsor is the lawyer of record throughout. (GRGAPL 8.01(e)(2), App. A(9))

docs.t: Guam — Judge challenge must come before the first fact hearing
docs.x: Guam land mine. Judge challenge must come before the first fact hearing: No peremptory challenge exists. A verified for-cause statement must be filed at the earliest practicable opportunity after you learn of the ground, and in all events before the hearing of any issue of fact starts. Waiting until after an adverse ruling at trial forfeits the challenge. (7 GCA § 6107(a)–(b))

docs.t: Guam — Appellate briefs: 14-point type, colored covers, excerpts of record in every case
docs.x: Guam land mine. Appellate briefs: 14-point type, colored covers, excerpts of record in every case: Proportional fonts must be 14-point or larger, with serifs in the text. Page and word limits: • Opening and answering briefs: 30 pages or 14,000 words. • Reply briefs: 15 pages or half the word count. • In cross-appeals, the appellee’s principal and response brief may run 35 pages or 16,500 words. The court disfavors motions to exceed the limits; file one at least 14 days before the brief is due (7 days for a reply). Covers are color-coded. Excerpts of record are required in every appeal (3 copies, filed with the opening brief). You may not incorporate trial-court briefs by reference. (GRAP 13.2(e), 15(a)–(b), 16(a)(2), (5), (7))

docs.t: Guam — Summary judgment: 30 days after discovery closes, with a statement of undisputed facts
docs.x: Guam land mine. Summary judgment: 30 days after discovery closes, with a statement of undisputed facts: Unless the court orders otherwise, summary judgment motions may be filed up to 30 days after the close of all discovery. A motion must include a statement of the issues and a separate “Statement of Undisputed Material Facts” with record citations. The opposing party must respond to that statement. (GRCP 56(b); CVR 56.1)

docs.t: Guam anti-SLAPP — Citizen Participation in Government Act of 1998 (7 GCA §§ 17101–17109)
docs.x: Guam anti-SLAPP. Citizen Participation in Government Act of 1998 (7 GCA §§ 17101–17109): Guam has an anti-SLAPP statute. It was enacted as uncodified P.L. 24-297 (Dec. 3, 1998) and codified by the Compiler as Chapter 17 of Title 7. Its core is an immunity: acts in furtherance of the constitutional right to petition, “including seeking relief, influencing action, informing, communicating and otherwise participating in the processes of government,” are immune from liability regardless of intent or purpose, unless they are not aimed at procuring any government or electoral action, result or outcome (§ 17104). “Government” includes officials and agencies of the United States, any state or territory, and the electorate (§ 17103(a)). Scope is petitioning, not all speech on public issues: unlike California-style statutes, there is no separate category for statements in a public forum on matters

docs.t: Guam anti-SLAPP — Procedure: summary-judgment motion, discovery stay, clear-and-convincing burden on the plaintiff
docs.x: Guam anti-SLAPP. Procedure: summary-judgment motion, discovery stay, clear-and-convincing burden on the plaintiff: The Act applies to any motion to dispose of a claim on the ground that it is based on, relates to, or responds to the movant’s protected petitioning (§ 17105). “Motion” is broad: a motion to dismiss, for summary judgment, for judgment on the pleadings, to strike, or any other filing to dispose of a claim (§ 17103(d)). Once filed: • the motion is treated as one for summary judgment, heard on the time frame used for preferred or expedited motions; • all discovery is suspended until the motion and any appeal are decided; • the responding party (the claimant) bears the burden of proof, of going forward, and of persuasion; • the court decides on the pleadings and affidavits; and • the court must grant the motion and dismiss unless the claimant produces clear and convincing eviden

docs.t: Guam anti-SLAPP — Mandatory fees and sanctions, plus a damages claim (SLAPP-back)
docs.x: Guam anti-SLAPP. Mandatory fees and sanctions, plus a damages claim (SLAPP-back): A moving party who wins dismissal must be awarded, “without regards to any limit under Guam law,” the costs of litigation including reasonable attorney and expert witness fees incurred on the motion. The court must also impose sanctions on the responding party, its attorneys or law firms sufficient to deter repetition (§ 17106(g)). Separately, a person harmed by a claim filed in violation of § 17104 may sue the persons responsible for actual or compensatory damages, punitive damages, attorney’s fees and costs (§ 17106(h)). (7 GCA § 17106(g)–(h))

docs.t: Guam anti-SLAPP — Appeal: expedited appeal of a denial, or of a failure to rule promptly
docs.x: Guam anti-SLAPP. Appeal: expedited appeal of a denial, or of a failure to rule promptly: The moving party has a right to an expedited appeal from an order denying the motion, or from the trial court’s failure to rule on it in expedited fashion (§ 17106(a)(2)). Discovery stays suspended during the appeal (§ 17106(b)). The collected Guam Rules of Appellate Procedure (2014 compilation) contain no rule specific to these appeals, so the notice of appeal timing in GRAP 4(a) (30 days from entry) is the safe assumption; ask for expedited treatment in the Supreme Court. (7 GCA § 17106(a)(2), (b); GRAP 4(a)(1))

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Notice of appeal, civil (filed in Superior Court)
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Notice of appeal, civil (filed in Superior Court): 30 days from Entry of the judgment or order appealed from (GRAP 4(a)(1), 3(a)). Jurisdictional. Pay the Supreme Court docket fee ($375 on posted schedule) at filing (GRAP 8(a)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Notice of appeal by another party / cross-appeal
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Notice of appeal by another party / cross-appeal: 14 days from Filing of the first notice of appeal (or the regular 30 days, if later) (GRAP 4(a)(3)). Cross-appellant pays its own docket fee.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Statement of jurisdiction
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Statement of jurisdiction: 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (GRAP 4.1(a)–(b)). Mandatory dismissal if not filed. GRAP 11 excludes weekends and holidays from periods under 11 days.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Order transcript or certify none; representation statement
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Order transcript or certify none; representation statement: 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (transcript: or decision on last tolling motion, if later) (GRAP 7(b)(1), 8(b)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Post-judgment motions (GRCP 50(b), 52(b), 59 new trial or alter/amend)
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Post-judgment motions (GRCP 50(b), 52(b), 59 new trial or alter/amend): 10 days from Entry of judgment (GRCP 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e); GRCP 6(b)(2)). Cannot be extended. Calendar days since Oct. 19, 2023 (GRCP 6(a)). Timely motion restarts appeal time (GRAP 4(a)(4)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Rule 60 motion that tolls appeal time
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Rule 60 motion that tolls appeal time: 10 days from Entry of judgment (GRAP 4(a)(4)(A)(vi)). Later Rule 60 motions (up to 1 year for reasons 1–3) do not toll.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Attorney’s fee motion
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Attorney’s fee motion: 14 days from Entry of judgment (GRCP 54(d)(2)(B); CVR 54.3). Tolls appeal time only if the court so orders under GRCP 58(c).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Motion to extend time to appeal
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Motion to extend time to appeal: 14 days from Expiration of the 30-day appeal period (GRAP 4(a)(5)). Excusable neglect or good cause. Extension capped at 30 days past the deadline or 10 days after the order, whichever is later.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Motion to reopen time to appeal
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Motion to reopen time to appeal: 180 days from Entry of judgment (or 7 days after receiving notice, if earlier) (GRAP 4(a)(6)). Only if notice of entry was not received within 21 days. Reopened window is 14 days.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Petition for permission to appeal (interlocutory)
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Petition for permission to appeal (interlocutory): 30 days from Entry of the order (unless the authorizing statute or rule sets another time) (GRAP 4.2(a)(2), 4(a)(1); 7 GCA § 3108(b)). Answer or cross-petition 7 days after service. 15-page limit.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Application to appeal class-certification order
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Application to appeal class-certification order: 10 days from Entry of the order (GRCP 23(f)). Discretionary. No automatic stay.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Opening brief and excerpts of record
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Opening brief and excerpts of record: 40 days from Filing of the record (certificate of record) (GRAP 17(a), 13.2(f)(1), 15(b), 7.1(c)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Answering brief
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Answering brief: 30 days from Service of the opening brief (GRAP 17(a), 13.2(f)(2)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Reply brief: 14 days from Service of the answering brief (GRAP 17(a)). Also at least 14 days before argument absent good cause. In a cross-appeal the appellant’s response-and-reply is due in 30 days and the appellee’s reply in 14 (GRAP 13.2(f)(3)–(4)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Motion to exceed page or word limits
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Motion to exceed page or word limits: 14 days from Before the brief’s due date (7 days for a reply) (GRAP 16(a)(7)(C)). Granted only for extraordinary and compelling reasons.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Written motion to extend a brief deadline
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Written motion to extend a brief deadline: 5 days from Before the brief’s due date (GRAP 17(c)(2)). One oral clerk extension of up to 14 days is available first (GRAP 17(c)(1)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Response to a motion
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Response to a motion: 7 days from Service of the motion (GRAP 6(a)(3)(A)). Non-opposition statement due in the same 7 days. Reply due 5 days after the response.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Amicus brief
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Amicus brief: 7 days from Filing of the supported party’s principal brief (GRAP 14(e)).

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Petition for rehearing (panel or en banc)
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing (panel or en banc): 14 days from Entry of judgment (GRAP 30(a)(1), 29(c)). 45 days in a civil case where the Government of Guam or its officer or agency is a party.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Issuance of mandate
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Issuance of mandate: 7 days from Expiration of rehearing time or denial of rehearing or stay motion (GRAP 27(c)(2)). Calendar days.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Bill of costs
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Bill of costs: 14 days from Entry of judgment (GRAP 22(d)(1)). Objections within 10 days after service.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Stay of mandate pending U.S. Supreme Court certiorari
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Stay of mandate pending U.S. Supreme Court certiorari: 90 days from Grant of the stay (GRAP 27(c)(4)(B)(ii)). Continues if the petition is filed and the Clerk notified within the stay.

docs.t: Guam appeal deadline — Criminal appeal by defendant (for reference)
docs.x: Guam appellate deadline. Criminal appeal by defendant (for reference): 10 days from Entry of judgment or order (or government’s notice, if later) (GRAP 4(b)(1)(A)). Government: 30 days (GRAP 4(b)(1)(B)).

docs.t: Hawaii — Answer in 20 days, not 21
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Answer in 20 days, not 21: An answer is due 20 days after service of the summons and complaint. After a Rule 12 motion is denied, the answer is due in 10 days. There is no waiver-of-service procedure that extends the deadline. (HRCP Rules 4, 12(a))

docs.t: Hawaii — Post-trial motions are due in 10 days
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Post-trial motions are due in 10 days: Renewed judgment-as-a-matter-of-law, amended-findings, and new-trial/alter-or-amend motions must be filed no later than 10 days after entry of judgment (federal: 28). The court cannot extend these deadlines. (HRCP Rules 6(b), 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e))

docs.t: Hawaii — The 90-day deemed-denial trap on tolling motions
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. The 90-day deemed-denial trap on tolling motions: A timely post-judgment tolling motion extends the appeal time, but if the court does not enter an order within 90 days the motion is denied by operation of the rule. Under the current rule, the appeal clock runs from the clerk’s notice of that denial. From January 1, 2027, with no filed written order within 90 days, the notice of appeal is due 120 days after the motion was filed, and a Rule 60(b) motion tolls only if filed within 30 days of judgment. (HRAP Rule 4(a)(3) (current; amended eff. Jan. 1, 2027))

docs.t: Hawaii — Motion practice runs on 18/8/3 days and page limits
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Motion practice runs on 18/8/3 days and page limits: Hearing motions must be filed and served at least 18 days before the hearing, oppositions at least 8 days, and replies at least 3 days. Mail service adds 2 days, not 3. Memoranda are capped at 20 pages (replies 10), and memoranda over 15 pages need tables of contents and authorities. (HRCP Rule 6(d)–(e); RCCH Rules 7(b), 7.1, 8)

docs.t: Hawaii — Dispositive motions die 50 days before trial
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Dispositive motions die 50 days before trial: Motions seeking judgment or dismissal of any claim, including summary judgment, must be filed no later than 50 days before the assigned trial date unless the court allows otherwise for good cause. (RCCH Rule 7(f); HRCP Rule 56(b))

docs.t: Hawaii — Serve within 6 months or risk dismissal
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Serve within 6 months or risk dismissal: HRCP has no 90-day service limit, but the court may dismiss any action or claim on its own, with written notice, if no service is made within 6 months after filing. A motion to reinstate must be filed within 10 days of the dismissal order. (RCCH Rule 28)

docs.t: Hawaii — Jury demand within 10 days
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Jury demand within 10 days: Serve a written jury demand no later than 10 days after service of the last pleading directed to the issue (federal: 14) and file it, or the jury right is waived. In district court, a jury demand sends the case to circuit court. (HRCP Rule 38(b), (d); HRS § 604-5(b))

docs.t: Hawaii — Don’t file defamation in district court
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Don’t file defamation in district court: District courts lack jurisdiction over libel, slander, defamation, malicious prosecution, false imprisonment, and real-property title disputes, whatever the amount. (HRS § 604-5(d))

docs.t: Hawaii — No temporary-practice safe harbor and no e-filing account
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. No temporary-practice safe harbor and no e-filing account: Hawai‘i Rule 5.5 has no ABA 5.5(c) temporary-practice exception, so out-of-state lawyers need pro hac vice even for limited court work. Pro hac vice counsel cannot register for JEFS, and local counsel must sign and file everything. (HRPC Rule 5.5; RSCH Rule 1.9(d); HEFSR Rule 4.1(a))

docs.t: Hawaii — Pay the pro hac vice fees within 10 days
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Pay the pro hac vice fees within 10 days: If the annual Disciplinary Board and Lawyers’ Fund fees are not paid, with proof filed, within 10 days after the order granting pro hac vice, the order is no longer valid and a new motion must be filed. Unpaid December renewals bring automatic suspension. (RSCH Rule 1.9(a)(2)–(3))

docs.t: Hawaii — ‘Non-refundable’ retainers are forbidden
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. ‘Non-refundable’ retainers are forbidden: No fee agreement may describe a fee as non-refundable or earned on receipt. Advance fees are presumed unearned and must be held in trust, and flat fees over $1,500 need a signed agreement with refund terms. (HRPC Rule 1.5(b)–(c))

docs.t: Hawaii — Appellate briefs are limited by pages, with strict points of error
docs.x: Hawaii land mine. Appellate briefs are limited by pages, with strict points of error: Opening and answering briefs are capped at 35 pages and replies at 10, in 12-point type. Each point of error must say where in the record the error occurred and where it was objected to (quoting the evidence, instruction, or finding at issue); nonconforming points are disregarded. Hawai‘i cases since statehood must be cited to both the state and regional reporters. (HRAP Rules 28(a), 28(b)(1), (4), 32(b))

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Hawaii Public Expression Protection Act (UPEPA)
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Hawaii Public Expression Protection Act (UPEPA): Hawai‘i adopted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act as HRS chapter 634G (L 2022, c 96). The older anti-SLAPP chapter, HRS ch. 634F (Citizen Participation in Government), was repealed by the same act. The effective date of Act 96 is not shown in the collected text, so check it for claims based on conduct around 2022. (HRS ch. 634G; HRS ch. 634F (repealed, L 2022, c 96, §3))

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Scope: three kinds of protected activity, three exclusions
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Scope: three kinds of protected activity, three exclusions: Covers claims based on (1) communication in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding; (2) communication on an issue under consideration in such a proceeding; or (3) exercise of free speech, press, assembly, petition, or association rights under the U.S. or Hawai‘i Constitution on a matter of public concern. Excluded: claims against a governmental unit or its employee acting officially; government enforcement actions against an imminent threat to public health or safety; and claims against a business arising from a communication about selling or leasing its goods or services (dramatic, literary, musical, political, journalistic, and artistic works are not ‘goods or services’). The official text misprints the section heading as ‘§643G-2’. (HRS § 634G-2)

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Special motion to dismiss: 60 days from service, and everything stops
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Special motion to dismiss: 60 days from service, and everything stops: File no later than 60 days after service of the pleading asserting the claim, or later for good cause, notwithstanding court rules. Filing automatically stays all other proceedings between the moving and responding parties, including discovery and pending motions; the court may also stay related proceedings involving other parties. The stay lasts until the order and the time to appeal it expire. Limited discovery is allowed only if specific information is needed to meet the dismissal burden and is not otherwise reasonably available. A fee motion, voluntary dismissal, severance, and good-cause rulings on unrelated motions or public-safety injunctions are not stayed. (HRS § 634G-3)

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Hearing within 60 days; ruling within 60 days after hearing
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Hearing within 60 days; ruling within 60 days after hearing: The court must hear the motion no later than 60 days after filing, unless it orders later for allowed discovery (then within 60 days after the discovery order) or other good cause, and must rule no later than 60 days after the hearing. The court considers the pleadings, motion papers, and any evidence admissible on summary judgment under the Hawai‘i Rules of Civil Procedure. (HRS §§ 634G-4, 634G-5, 634G-7)

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Three-step test; dismissal is with prejudice
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Three-step test; dismissal is with prejudice: The court must dismiss with prejudice if the movant shows the chapter applies, the responding party fails to show an exclusion, and either the responding party fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the movant’s right to a ruling and fees; a voluntary dismissal with prejudice means the movant prevailed for fee purposes. (HRS § 634G-6)

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Mandatory fees for a winning movant
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Mandatory fees for a winning movant: The court ‘shall award’ costs, reasonable attorney’s fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a prevailing movant. A prevailing responding party gets them only if the court finds the motion frivolous or filed solely to delay. (HRS § 634G-9)

docs.t: Hawaii anti-SLAPP — Immediate appeal of a denial, 30 days, with a full stay
docs.x: Hawaii anti-SLAPP. Immediate appeal of a denial, 30 days, with a full stay: A moving party may appeal as of right within 30 days from an order denying the motion in whole or in part. While that appeal is pending, all proceedings between all parties are stayed. The Act must be construed liberally to protect speech, press, assembly, petition, and association rights, with attention to uniformity among enacting states. (HRS §§ 634G-3(d), 634G-8, 634G-10, 634G-11)

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil): 30 days from Entry (filing) of the judgment or appealable order (HRAP 4(a)(1)). Jurisdictional. Mailed notice timely if postmarked in time and received within 5 days. File the Civil Appeal Docketing Statement with it.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Proof of service of notice of appeal
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Proof of service of notice of appeal: 7 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (HRAP 3(e)(1)).

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Motion for leave for interlocutory appeal (circuit court)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Motion for leave for interlocutory appeal (circuit court): 30 days from Entry of the interlocutory order (HRAP 4(a)(1); HRS § 641-1(b)). If granted, the notice of appeal is due 30 days after entry of the order granting leave.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Renewed JMOL / amend findings / new trial / alter or amend
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Renewed JMOL / amend findings / new trial / alter or amend: 10 days from Entry of judgment (HRCP 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e)). Cannot be extended (HRCP 6(b)). A timely motion tolls the appeal time.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Notice of appeal after a tolling motion
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Notice of appeal after a tolling motion: 30 days from Entry of the order deciding the motion (or the clerk’s deemed-denial notice) (HRAP 4(a)(3) (current)). The court must rule within 90 days of the motion; otherwise it is deemed denied. From Jan. 1, 2027: 30 days after a filed written order entered within 90 days, otherwise 120 days after the motion was filed.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Extension of time for notice of appeal
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Extension of time for notice of appeal: 30 days from Expiration of the original appeal period (HRAP 4(a)(4)). Motion in the court appealed from: good cause if filed before expiry, excusable neglect if filed within 30 days after. Extension capped at 30 days past the original deadline.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Cross-appeal
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Cross-appeal: 14 days from Service of the notice of appeal on the cross-appellant (HRAP 4.1(b)(1)). Or within the time for the notice of appeal, whichever is later.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Transcript request (or certificate that none needed)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Transcript request (or certificate that none needed): 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (HRAP 10(b)(1)(A)).

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Request for findings of fact/conclusions of law (where required after appeal)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Request for findings of fact/conclusions of law (where required after appeal): 10 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (HRAP 10(f)). The judge must enter them within 28 days of the request.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Record on appeal filed by clerk below
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Record on appeal filed by clerk below: 60 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (HRAP 11(b)(1)).

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Statement of jurisdiction
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Statement of jurisdiction: 10 days from Filing of the record on appeal (HRAP 12.1(a)). 10-page limit. Appellees contesting jurisdiction file within the same period.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Opening brief
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Opening brief: 40 days from Filing of the record on appeal (HRAP 28(b)). 35-page limit. One clerk extension of up to 30 days on a timely request (HRAP 29(a)).

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Answering brief
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Answering brief: 40 days from Service of the opening brief (or docketing, if later) (HRAP 28(c)). 35-page limit. One clerk extension of up to 30 days.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Reply brief
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Reply brief: 14 days from Service of the answering brief (HRAP 28(d)). 10-page limit. One clerk extension of up to 10 days. If not filing, notify the clerk before the deadline.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Motion for further brief extension
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Motion for further brief extension: 5 days from Before the brief’s due date (at least) (HRAP 29(b)). Good cause required. Does not toll the deadline.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Motion to disqualify appellate judge/justice
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Motion to disqualify appellate judge/justice: 10 days from Opening of the appellate proceeding or discovery of new information (HRAP 5(b)). Otherwise waived absent good cause.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Motion for reconsideration (appellate)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Motion for reconsideration (appellate): 10 days from Filing of the opinion, dispositional order, or ruling (HRAP 40(a)). If the court does not act within 10 days, the motion is rejected. One motion per party.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Request for appellate fees and costs
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Request for appellate fees and costs: 14 days from Expiration of the reconsideration period or decision on reconsideration (HRAP 39(d)(2)). Objections due in 10 days, replies in 7 (HRAP 39(d)(4)).

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Application for writ of certiorari
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Application for writ of certiorari: 30 days from Filing of the ICA judgment on appeal or dismissal order (HRAP 40.1(a)(1); HRS § 602-59(c)). A written request filed within the 30 days gets an automatic 30-day extension. 20-page limit.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Response to certiorari application
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Response to certiorari application: 15 days from Filing of the application (HRAP 40.1(e)(1)). Optional. Automatic 15-day extension on timely request. Reply within 7 days, 5 pages.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Supreme Court action on certiorari
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Supreme Court action on certiorari: 60 days from Filing of the application (HRAP 40.1(g)). No acceptance within 60 days = rejection.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Application for transfer to Supreme Court (latest)
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Application for transfer to Supreme Court (latest): 20 days from Filing (or due date) of the last brief (HRAP 40.2(a)(2)). Not earlier than 10 days after the record is filed. Response 10 days. Decision within 45 days. No extensions.

docs.t: Hawaii appeal deadline — Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP motion
docs.x: Hawaii appellate deadline. Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP motion: 30 days from Order denying the special motion to dismiss (HRS § 634G-8). As of right. All proceedings are stayed pending appeal (HRS § 634G-3(d)).

docs.t: Iowa — No default without a 10-day mailed notice of intent
docs.x: Iowa land mine. No default without a 10-day mailed notice of intent: Before applying for a default, mail written notice of intent to the defaulting party and to any lawyer you know represents it, at least 10 days before filing the application. The days run from mailing. The application must certify the notice and attach a copy (Form 10). Exceptions: small claims, eviction (forcible entry and detainer), juvenile cases, and service by publication. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.972(2)–(4))

docs.t: Iowa — Do not plead a dollar amount; say ‘law’ or ‘equity’
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Do not plead a dollar amount; say ‘law’ or ‘equity’: Except in small claims and liquidated-damages cases, a pleading may not state the specific amount of money damages sought. It states only whether the amount meets jurisdictional requirements. The petition must also state whether the action is at law or in equity, which affects trial and appellate review (equity cases are reviewed de novo). (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.403(1)–(2); Iowa R. App. P. 6.907)

docs.t: Iowa — Post-trial motions are due 15 days after the decision is filed
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Post-trial motions are due 15 days after the decision is filed: Not 28 days after judgment as in federal court. Motions for new trial and JNOV, and a Rule 1.904(2) motion to amend findings, are due 15 days after the verdict, report, or decision is filed. The court may extend by at most 30 days, for good cause and not ex parte. Only a timely motion restarts the appeal clock, and a second such motion by the same party does not. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.904(2), 1.1007; Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(1)(b)–(c))

docs.t: Iowa — Appeal: 30 days, filed in the district court, then 7-day follow-ups
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Appeal: 30 days, filed in the district court, then 7-day follow-ups: The notice of appeal goes to the district court clerk, with an informational copy to the supreme court, within 30 days after the judgment is filed. The appellate courts cannot extend this. Within 7 more days you must pay the $150 fee and file and serve the combined certificate ordering the transcript. (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(1)(b), 6.102(3), 6.804(1), 6.1003(1))

docs.t: Iowa — Further review: 20 days, and rehearing does not stop the clock
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Further review: 20 days, and rehearing does not stop the clock: An application for supreme court review of a Court of Appeals decision is due 20 days after the decision is filed, and the supreme court cannot extend it. A petition for rehearing in the Court of Appeals (due in 7 days) does not toll the 20 days, so file both if needed. (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1003(1)(e), 6.1103(1)(a), 6.1204(1)–(2))

docs.t: Iowa — Preserve error and say how in the brief
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Preserve error and say how in the brief: Each argument must open with a statement of how the issue was preserved, with record cites to where it was raised and decided below. Citing the notice of appeal is not enough. Uncited issues may be deemed waived. Each missed appellate deadline brings a $150 penalty that the lawyer pays personally. (Iowa R. App. P. 6.903(2)(a)(8), 6.1202(2))

docs.t: Iowa — Serve within 90 days of filing
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Serve within 90 days of filing: If the original notice is not served within 90 days after the petition is filed, the court must dismiss without prejudice as to that defendant, or direct another time or manner of service, unless good cause is shown. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.302(5))

docs.t: Iowa — Old cases are swept every year
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Old cases are swept every year: A case whose petition was filed more than one year before July 15 must be tried before January 1 of the next year, or it is dismissed without prejudice at the plaintiff’s cost. The clerk sends notice by August 15. A continuance requires a court order; a stipulation alone does not work. Reinstatement must be sought within six months. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.944(2), (5)–(6))

docs.t: Iowa — $1,000 late-settlement fee
docs.x: Iowa land mine. $1,000 late-settlement fee: Waiving a jury or settling later than two full working days before a scheduled jury trial, or settling during trial, brings a $1,000 fee assessed as court costs. The court may not waive it or grant a continuance to avoid it. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.909)

docs.t: Iowa — Only 60 days to set aside a default judgment
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Only 60 days to set aside a default judgment: A motion to set aside a default or default judgment for mistake, inadvertence, surprise, excusable neglect, or unavoidable casualty must be filed promptly after the grounds are discovered, and never more than 60 days after entry of the judgment. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.977)

docs.t: Iowa — Discovery conference within 21 days of the first answer, even with a motion pending
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Discovery conference within 21 days of the first answer, even with a motion pending: The parties must confer no later than 21 days after any defendant answers or appears. A pending pre-answer motion does not suspend the conference or initial disclosures. (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.507(1))

docs.t: Iowa — Pro hac vice is case-by-case and filed by Iowa counsel
docs.x: Iowa land mine. Pro hac vice is case-by-case and filed by Iowa counsel: Register and pay $250 with the Office of Professional Regulation first. Your Iowa co-counsel files the application electronically, and you can e-file only after it is granted. Admission does not carry over to the appeal: apply again in each later district or appellate proceeding. After five admissions in two years, you must show good cause. (Iowa Ct. R. 31.14(2)(c), 31.14(7)(d), 31.14(11); Iowa R. Elec. P. 16.304(1)(b)(1))

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Iowa adopted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act in 2025
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Iowa adopted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act in 2025: Iowa Code chapter 652 (2025 Iowa Acts ch. 93) applies to civil actions filed on or after July 1, 2025. It covers claims based on: (a) communications in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding; (b) communications on an issue under consideration or review in such a proceeding; or (c) exercise of the federal or Iowa rights of free speech, press, assembly, petition, or association on a matter of public concern. The act must be construed broadly to protect those rights. (Iowa Code §§ 652.1, 652.2(2), 652.11; 2025 Iowa Acts ch. 93, § 13)

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Only three exclusions
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Only three exclusions: The act does not apply to claims (a) against a governmental unit, or its employee or agent acting or purporting to act officially; (b) by a governmental unit or its official enforcing a law against an imminent threat to public health or safety; or (c) against a person primarily engaged in selling or leasing goods or services, where the claim arises from a communication related to that sale or lease. ‘Goods or services’ excludes creating, disseminating, exhibiting, or advertising dramatic, literary, musical, political, journalistic, or artistic works. The collected text lists no other exclusions. (Iowa Code § 652.2(1), (3))

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Procedure: special motion within 60 days; automatic stay
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Procedure: special motion within 60 days; automatic stay: File a special motion for expedited relief within 60 days after being served with the pleading asserting the claim, or later for good cause. Filing stays all other proceedings between the moving and responding parties, including discovery, until the ruling and the time to appeal it expire. The court may allow limited, specific discovery and may hear unrelated motions or emergency injunction motions. The hearing must be held within 60 days after the motion is filed, or within 60 days after an order allowing discovery, unless the court orders a later hearing for good cause. The ruling is due within 60 days after the hearing. A voluntary dismissal does not end the stay’s purpose: the movant can still get a ruling and fees. (Iowa Code §§ 652.3, 652.4, 652.5, 652.8)

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Standard: three-step test, dismissal with prejudice
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Standard: three-step test, dismissal with prejudice: The court considers the pleadings, the motion, any reply or response, and evidence that could be considered on summary judgment under Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.981. It must dismiss with prejudice if: (1) the movant shows the act applies; (2) the responding party fails to show an exclusion applies; and (3) either the responding party fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim, or no genuine issue of material fact. A voluntary dismissal with prejudice means the movant prevailed for fee purposes. (Iowa Code §§ 652.6, 652.7)

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Fees are mandatory
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Fees are mandatory: The court shall award court costs, reasonable attorney fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a moving party who prevails. A responding party gets them only if it prevails and the court finds the motion frivolous or filed solely to delay. A fee motion is not subject to the stay. (Iowa Code §§ 652.4(5), 652.10)

docs.t: Iowa anti-SLAPP — Immediate appeal within 30 days, with a stay
docs.x: Iowa anti-SLAPP. Immediate appeal within 30 days, with a stay: A moving party may appeal as of right from an order denying the motion in whole or in part, within 30 days after entry. While the appeal is pending, all proceedings between all parties are stayed. Under the appellate rules, an appeal authorized by statute is taken by notice of appeal that names the statute. (Iowa Code §§ 652.4(3), 652.9; Iowa R. App. P. 6.108)

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (final order or judgment)
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (final order or judgment): 30 days from Filing of the final order or judgment (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(1)(b)). Filed in the district court with an informational copy to the supreme court. Not extendable except for the clerk’s failure to give notice (Rule 6.101(5)).

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Notice of appeal after a timely Rule 1.904(2) or 1.1007 motion
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Notice of appeal after a timely Rule 1.904(2) or 1.1007 motion: 30 days from Filing of the ruling on the motion (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(1)(b)–(c)). A successive motion by the same party does not count unless it addresses only a modification.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Notice of appeal in chapter 232 CINA or termination cases
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Notice of appeal in chapter 232 CINA or termination cases: 15 days from Filing of the order or judgment (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(1)(a)). Amendments effective January 1, 2027 change juvenile appeal rules; check the new text.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Notice of cross-appeal
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Notice of cross-appeal: 30 days from Filing of the final order, or 10 days after the notice of appeal, whichever is later (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(2)(b)). 15-day base period in chapter 232 cases.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Motion to extend appeal time for lack of clerk notice
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Motion to extend appeal time for lack of clerk notice: 60 days from Expiration of the original appeal deadline (Iowa R. App. P. 6.101(5)). Any extension granted runs no more than 30 days after the order granting it.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Filing fee and combined certificate
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Filing fee and combined certificate: 7 days from Filing of the notice of appeal (Iowa R. App. P. 6.102(3), 6.804(1)). $150 fee. Certificate to both clerks and to court reporters.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Transcript filed by court reporter
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Transcript filed by court reporter: 40 days from Service of the combined certificate (Iowa R. App. P. 6.803). 20 days for guilty pleas and sentencing; 30 days in chapter 232 cases.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Appellant’s brief
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Appellant’s brief: 50 days from Clerk’s notice of briefing deadline (Iowa R. App. P. 6.901(1)(a)). Halved in expedited cases (Rule 6.902).

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Appellee’s brief
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Appellee’s brief: 30 days from Service of the appellant’s brief (Iowa R. App. P. 6.901(1)(b)). Or a written statement waiving the brief.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Appellant’s reply brief
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Appellant’s reply brief: 21 days from Service of the appellee’s brief (Iowa R. App. P. 6.901(1)(c)). With a cross-appeal the appellant must reply or file a waiver; the cross-appellant then has 14 days to reply.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Resistance to a motion
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Resistance to a motion: 14 days from Service of the motion (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1002(2)). Reply within 3 days after the resistance.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Cure of default after clerk’s notice
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Cure of default after clerk’s notice: 15 days from Issuance of the default notice (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1202(1)). $150 penalty to the lawyer for each default notice.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Application for interlocutory appeal
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Application for interlocutory appeal: 30 days from Entry of the ruling (or of the ruling on a timely 1.904(2) motion) (Iowa R. App. P. 6.104(1)(c)). 15 days in chapter 232 cases.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Petition for writ of certiorari
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Petition for writ of certiorari: 30 days from Entry of the challenged decision (Iowa R. App. P. 6.107(1)(b)). Runs from the ruling on a timely 1.904(2) or 1.1007 motion.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Application for discretionary review
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Application for discretionary review: 30 days from Entry of the ruling, order, or judgment (Iowa R. App. P. 6.106(1)(b)).

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Petition for rehearing in the Court of Appeals
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing in the Court of Appeals: 7 days from Filing of the Court of Appeals decision (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1204(2)). Does not toll the 20-day further-review period.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Application for further review
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Application for further review: 20 days from Filing of the Court of Appeals decision (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1103(1)(a)(2)). 10 days in chapter 232 cases. Not extendable by the supreme court.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Resistance to application for further review
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Resistance to application for further review: 10 days from Service of the application (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1103(2)(b)). No replies. Not permitted in chapter 232 cases unless requested.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Petition for rehearing in the supreme court
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Petition for rehearing in the supreme court: 14 days from Filing of the supreme court opinion (Iowa R. App. P. 6.1205(1)). Unless the court shortens or enlarges the time.

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP motion
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Appeal from denial of anti-SLAPP motion: 30 days from Entry of the order (Iowa Code § 652.9). Moving party only; proceedings are stayed during the appeal (§ 652.4(3)).

docs.t: Iowa appeal deadline — Motion for new trial or JNOV (trial court)
docs.x: Iowa appellate deadline. Motion for new trial or JNOV (trial court): 15 days from Filing of the verdict, report, or decision (Iowa R. Civ. P. 1.1007). Court may add up to 30 days for good cause, not ex parte.

docs.t: Idaho — Disqualification without cause can expire within 7 days
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Disqualification without cause can expire within 7 days: The peremptory motion is due 7 days after service of the first notice setting a status conference, pretrial conference, trial, or contested motion hearing, if that comes before the 21-day pleading deadline. It is lost once the judge presides over any such proceeding. Each party gets only one in the case. (I.R.C.P. 40(a)(1), (4))

docs.t: Idaho — Notice of appeal: 42 days from the file stamp, filed in the trial court, jurisdictional
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Notice of appeal: 42 days from the file stamp, filed in the trial court, jurisdictional: Appeal by filing a notice with the district court clerk within 42 days from the clerk’s filing stamp on the judgment, not 30 days from entry or service. It is not filed until received, it cannot be extended, and a late notice means automatic dismissal. Rule 60 motions and cost or fee motions do not restart the clock. (I.A.R. 14(a), 20, 21, 46)

docs.t: Idaho — Post-judgment motions are due in 14 days, not 28
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Post-judgment motions are due in 14 days, not 28: Motions for new trial, to alter or amend, to amend findings, and for judgment notwithstanding the verdict are all due within 14 days after entry of judgment. A motion to reconsider an interlocutory order must come before, or within 14 days after, final judgment. The court cannot extend these times. (I.R.C.P. 50(b), 52(b), 59(b), (e), 11.2(b), 2.2(b))

docs.t: Idaho — A judgment must be a bare separate document
docs.x: Idaho land mine. A judgment must be a bare separate document: A judgment must be titled “Judgment” or “Decree,” begin “JUDGMENT IS ENTERED AS FOLLOWS:”, and contain no recitals, reasoning, or findings. It is final only if it resolves all claims as to all parties (except costs and fees) or carries a Rule 54(b) certificate. A nonconforming order may not start the appeal clock. (I.R.C.P. 54(a)-(b), 58; I.A.R. 11(a)(1), (3))

docs.t: Idaho — Costs and fees memorandum due 14 days after judgment, or waived
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Costs and fees memorandum due 14 days after judgment, or waived: File and serve the memorandum of costs and attorney fees, with an attorney affidavit, no later than 14 days after entry of judgment. Objections are due 14 days after service. On appeal, fees must be claimed as an issue in your first brief, and the costs memorandum is due 14 days after the opinion. (I.R.C.P. 54(d)(4)-(5), (e)(5); I.A.R. 40(c), 41(a), (d))

docs.t: Idaho — No automatic 30-day stay of judgment, and only 14 days after appeal
docs.x: Idaho land mine. No automatic 30-day stay of judgment, and only 14 days after appeal: Unlike the federal rule, Idaho has no automatic stay after entry of judgment; execution may issue at once unless the court orders otherwise. Filing a civil notice of appeal stays proceedings and execution for only 14 days. A stay of a money judgment needs a bond or cash deposit of the judgment plus 36%. (I.R.C.P. 62(a); I.A.R. 13(a), 13(b)(15))

docs.t: Idaho — Motion practice runs on a 14/7/2-day schedule tied to the hearing
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Motion practice runs on a 14/7/2-day schedule tied to the hearing: A motion, supporting affidavits and briefs, and the notice of hearing must be filed and served so they are received at least 14 days before the hearing. Opposition is due at least 7 days before, and a reply at least 2 days before. The motion must say whether oral argument is wanted and whether a brief will be filed. Summary judgment instead runs 28/14/7 days before the hearing, and the motion must be filed at least 90 days before trial. (I.R.C.P. 7(b)(3), 56(b))

docs.t: Idaho — Do not plead punitive damages
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Do not plead punitive damages: A complaint with a prayer for punitive damages violates the statute. Move to amend later, after showing at a hearing a reasonable likelihood of proving punitive damages at trial. (Idaho Code § 6-1604(2))

docs.t: Idaho — Fee demand letters before suing on small claims
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Fee demand letters before suing on small claims: To recover fees in actions pleading $35,000 or less, the plaintiff must send a written demand at least 10 days before filing. For personal injury, the demand and an itemized statement of claim with records must reach the insurer (or the defendant) at least 60 days before filing, and new injuries or damage items later waive fees. (Idaho Code § 12-120(1), (4))

docs.t: Idaho — Do not contact the other side’s retained expert
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Do not contact the other side’s retained expert: Idaho’s discovery rule bars contacting a retained expert disclosed by another party without that party’s permission or a court order. Discovery scope still uses “reasonably calculated to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence,” and the text contains no mandatory initial-disclosure requirement. (I.R.C.P. 26(b)(1), 26(b)(4))

docs.t: Idaho — Every caption needs an Idaho Bar number, and appellate papers need an Idaho signer
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Every caption needs an Idaho Bar number, and appellate papers need an Idaho signer: The attorney of record’s name, address, phone, email, and current Idaho State Bar number must appear above the court’s title on the first page. In the appellate courts, at least one licensed Idaho attorney of record must sign every notice, motion, petition, and brief. Pro hac vice local counsel must attend all court proceedings unless excused. (I.R.C.P. 2(a)(4); I.A.R. 11.2(a); I.B.C.R. 227(b)(2))

docs.t: Idaho — Rule 60(b) has a 6-month outer limit
docs.x: Idaho land mine. Rule 60(b) has a 6-month outer limit: A motion for relief from judgment for mistake, excusable neglect, newly discovered evidence, or fraud must be made within a reasonable time and no more than 6 months after entry of the judgment. The federal rule allows up to one year. (I.R.C.P. 60(c)(1))

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Statute: Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (effective January 1, 2026)
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Statute: Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (effective January 1, 2026): Idaho adopted the Uniform Public Expression Protection Act (UPEPA) in 2025, effective January 1, 2026. It applies to civil actions filed, and causes of action asserted, on or after January 1, 2026; claims asserted earlier are not affected. Before this Act, the Idaho Code chapter list shows no general anti-SLAPP statute. (Idaho Code §§ 6-3901, 6-3913, 6-3914 (2025 Idaho Sess. Laws ch. 17, § 1))

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Scope: three kinds of protected activity
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Scope: three kinds of protected activity: Covers any cause of action (including a cross-claim, counterclaim, or third-party claim) against a person based on: (a) communication in a legislative, executive, judicial, administrative, or other governmental proceeding; (b) communication on an issue under consideration or review in such a proceeding; or (c) exercise of freedom of speech or press, assembly, petition, or association under the U.S. or Idaho Constitution on a matter of public concern. Exclusions: claims against a governmental unit or its employees or agents acting officially; government enforcement actions against an imminent threat to public health or safety; and claims against a seller or lessor of goods or services arising from a communication about its own goods or services. Creating or promoting dramatic, literary, musical, political, journalistic, or artist

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Procedure: 60 days to file, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Procedure: 60 days to file, automatic stay, 60-day hearing and ruling: File a special motion for expedited relief within 60 days after being served with the pleading that asserts the claim, or later for good cause. Filing automatically stays all other proceedings between the movant and the responding party, including discovery and pending hearings or motions, until the court rules and the time to appeal runs; on motion, the court may also stay related matters involving other parties. Limited discovery is allowed only if specific information is needed to meet a burden and is not otherwise reasonably available. The court must hear the motion within 60 days after filing (later for allowed discovery or other good cause) and rule within 60 days after the hearing. Not stayed: fee motions, voluntary dismissals, severance, and, for good cause, unrelated motions and public-safet

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Standard: dismissal with prejudice
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Standard: dismissal with prejudice: The court considers the pleadings, the motion papers, and any evidence that could be considered on summary judgment. It must dismiss with prejudice if the movant shows the Act applies, the responding party fails to show an exclusion, and either the responding party fails to establish a prima facie case on each essential element, or the movant shows failure to state a claim or no genuine issue of material fact. A voluntary dismissal without prejudice does not defeat the motion or fees; a voluntary dismissal with prejudice makes the movant the prevailing party. (Idaho Code §§ 6-3906, 6-3907)

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Fees: mandatory for a prevailing movant
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Fees: mandatory for a prevailing movant: The court must award court costs, reasonable attorney’s fees, and reasonable litigation expenses related to the motion to a prevailing movant, and to a prevailing responding party only if the court finds the motion frivolous or filed solely to delay. (Idaho Code § 6-3910)

docs.t: Idaho anti-SLAPP — Appeal: as of right within 42 days, with a full stay
docs.x: Idaho anti-SLAPP. Appeal: as of right within 42 days, with a full stay: A moving party may appeal as of right from an order denying the motion in whole or in part, within 42 days after entry of the order “pursuant to applicable court rule.” While the appeal is pending, all proceedings between all parties are stayed. The Idaho Appellate Rules collected on November 10, 2026 do not mention the Act; the appeal would rest on I.A.R. 11(a)(8) (orders made appealable by statute), and the notice must cite the statute in its jurisdictional statement. (Idaho Code §§ 6-3904(3), 6-3909; I.A.R. 11(a)(8), 17(g))

docs.t: Idaho appeal deadline — Notice of appeal (civil, as of right)
docs.x: Idaho appellate deadline. Notice of appeal (civil, as of right): 42 days from Clerk’s filing stamp on the judgment or order (I.A.R. 14(a), 21).
